articles.title: El ‘Cara al Sol’ vuelve a sonar en las fiestas de un pueblo de Madrid y desata la polémica
articles.standfirst: El himno falangista se reprodujo en plena Plaza de España de Moraleja de Enmedio
articles.summary: El himno falangista se reprodujo en plena Plaza de España de Moraleja de Enmedio
articles.body: Las fiestas patronales de Moraleja de Enmedio han vuelto a quedar marcadas por la polémica después de que el conocido como ‘Cara al Sol’ sonara en plena Plaza de España, frente al Ayuntamiento, tras el pregón que daba comienzo a las celebraciones. El episodio tuvo lugar durante la noche del pasado sábado 5 de septiembre, cuando la plaza se encontraba llena de vecinos. La canción, vinculada históricamente a Falange, fue reproducida después del pregón y el chupinazo y antes de la verbena popular. Según varios testimonios recogidos por medios locales, algunos asistentes mostraron su malestar y pidieron que se detuviera la música. La respuesta que habrían recibido, según estos testigos, fue: “Lo apagáis vosotros”. El episodio ha provocado nuevas críticas hacia la gestión del Ayuntamiento. El PSOE de Moraleja de Enmedio ha denunciado públicamente la reproducción del himno y ha pedido explicaciones al Gobierno municipal, al considerar especialmente grave que ocurriera en un espacio público y durante uno de los principales actos de las fiestas. No es, ni mucho menos, la primera vez que el ‘Cara al Sol’ aparece durante las celebraciones del municipio. La polémica se remonta varios años atrás y ha estado especialmente relacionada con la peña taurina El Apretón, a la que los socialistas señalan por haber reproducido la canción en anteriores desfiles. En 2013, además, una bandera franquista llegó a exhibirse desde el balcón del Ayuntamiento, un episodio que también generó una fuerte controversia. La situación volvió a repetirse en años posteriores. En 2025, el PSOE ya denunció la reproducción del ‘Cara al Sol’ durante las fiestas y recordó que la alcaldesa, Arantxa Godino, había manifestado su malestar y asegurado que existía una orden para impedir que la canción se emitiera en la vía pública. En esta ocasión, sin embargo, el escenario ha elevado todavía más la controversia. El hecho de que la canción sonara frente al Ayuntamiento y justo después del pregón, con la plaza abarrotada, ha vuelto a colocar al municipio madrileño en el centro del debate político. El PSOE reclama que el Gobierno local explique qué ocurrió y qué medidas se adoptaron, mientras la polémica continúa generando reacciones entre los vecinos y en redes sociales.

articles.title: 9/11 showed we must always be looking toward the next threat

Twenty-five years ago, the 9/11 terrorist attacks killed 2,977 people and left us with profound questions about our security that redound to this day. The 9/11 Commission Report , a best-selling book at the time, explained how failures of imagination, management, capability and policy contributed to our failure to prevent the attacks. The existing national security system at that time had been built for Cold War threats — fighter aircraft, tanks, uniformed soldiers and conventional warfare. But a new threat had emerged, utilizing truck bombs, training recruits in caves and manipulating technology to battle in asymmetric environments. Al Qaeda, a regional terrorist group, had been deploying new challenges to the U.S. around the world throughout the 1990s. It attacked U.S. embassies in Africa with truck bombs and hit the USS Cole with explosives in a small boat. It also attempted to topple a building in New York City . U.S. security policies did not adapt fast enough, nor did our institutions change quickly enough, to counter a dynamic adversary testing our aging and vulnerable defenses. The bipartisan 9/11 Commission, led by Republican Chairman Tom Kean and Democratic Vice Chair Lee Hamilton, faced long odds on a polarized Capitol Hill and before a frightened public. After working with Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) to create the 9/11 Commission, I found myself serving on it and keenly recognized our time and budget constraints. Like most blue-ribbon commissions, we had very limited time. Even if we figured out the answers, we would face the significant problem of trying to pass our policy recommendations into law. Fortunately, we had several wise policy makers on the commission, with legislative experience in state and federal government, and a highly talented non-partisan staff. Importantly, we also had support from the 9/11 family members in New York, New Jersey and Virginia. They did the important and praiseworthy work of holding our feet to the fire, insisting on full accountability and transparency. And once we had finished, they relentlessly and energetically pushed members of Congress and the White House to embrace our policy recommendations and pass them into law. The 9/11 Commission proposed more than three dozen major policy recommendations. New and more agile organizations were created; many old stovepipes and bureaucratic structures were eliminated; and a multi-layered joint federal-state-local architecture was set up to encourage sharing information and integrating intelligence. The Director of National Intelligence was created to coordinate and manage the 17 various intelligence agencies across the government — to execute on long-term strategy and keep short-term politics out of the national security equation. The commission also recommended establishment of a National Counterterrorism Center staffed with experienced personnel from various agencies to enforce the practice of joint duty. We could not afford to have the FBI and CIA not sharing sensitive information with each other. REAL IDs were proposed across all 50 states for improving security, and the FBI instructed to build a new national security workforce with broad linguistic skills and deep analytical abilities. Aviation security was paramount, since the terrorists had repeatedly targeted aircraft. Screening systems that prevent suspects from boarding planes or entering the country were included in our extensive commercial airline travel system for the first time. There were about 16 names on the “No-Fly List” prior to 9/11 — today that list today includes thousands, and TSA officers provide a vital national security function. Early on, we discussed legislative strategy to engage Congress and persuade a skeptical White House to support our proposals. The 9/11 family organizations swarmed the Hill and invaded offices to persuade members to vote for our new ideas. Bipartisan leadership also stepped up in Congress. Sens. McCain, Susan Collins (R-Maine), Joe Lieberman (D-Conn.) and House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) were all key to formulating and passing the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004, which President George W. Bush signed into law. To this day, our new system has performed well — we have not experienced another such attack. But Congress failed to enact a key proposal for itself. Experts informed the commission that Congress that 92 various committees and subcommittees maintained some jurisdiction over homeland security. When everyone claims oversight, no one really has responsibility. Threats continue to evolve as corporations, universities, critical infrastructure and electrical and water grids are all experiencing cyberattacks. Last month, seven states reported serious attacks on water and utility related infrastructure. Iran, China, and Russia are likely culprits — all have serious capabilities in this area and a recent history of launching cyberattacks against the U.S. If the 9/11 attacks hit our airport infrastructure, today’s soft underbelly is our digital infrastructure. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency was created in 2019 to protect us from this threat, but it currently has only an acting director (not confirmed) and its professional staff has been reduced by one-third . The Iran War invites more cybersecurity concerns for the homeland as we interface with old infrastructure to protect our current systems from new forms of attack. This brings us to the question at the heart of 9/11: How do we anticipate the next set of threats before the next major attack takes place? We discovered in our work on the 9/11 Commission that our government had missed clues showing the new set of al Qaeda threats. So we must now ask again: Is the national security system constructed after 9/11 in need of updating, moderate reform or a complete overhaul? New tactics and tools change the very nature of war. The battle between Ukraine and Russia is demonstrating the future to us utilizing AI, robots and drone swarms. It is also underscoring the necessity for fundamentally altering our outdated defense procurement system and proposing budgets that are strong yet smart. The modernization of China’s military is a top focus for us. Terrorism has not gone away but continues to skew toward proxies, asymmetrical threats and cyberattacks. Hypersonic weapons, space and biosecurity will increase in importance. Deep fakes and disinformation campaigns by foreign adversaries heighten domestic polarization and domestic radicalization concerns. The conflict with Iran shows us the limits of lethality and the vital importance of geography. The 9/11 Commission heard compelling and riveting stories from people describing their fears of a potential attack prior to 9/11. Former CIA Director George Tenet said he felt like his “hair was on fire,” given a heightened level of possible terror activity. Richard Clarke, the National Security Advisor for President Bush, speculated in a Presidential Daily Brief about an attack and titled the memo “Bin Laden Determined to Attack Inside the United States.” Yes, we must never forget 9/11, but that is not enough on its own. We must constantly look ahead to where the next major plot will unfold. The alarm bells are ringing once again — let us act now to build a more resilient national security strategy moving forward. articles.title: Massachusetts' highest court publicly reprimands judge accused of enabling immigrant to escape ICE
articles.summary: Judge Shelley Joseph was publicly rebuked after an illegal immigrant evaded Immigration and Customs Enforcement in her Massachusetts courtroom.
articles.body: The highest court in Massachusetts has publicly rebuked a district court judge over her role in a case involving an illegal immigrant who evaded arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. For Judge Shelley Joseph, the decision brings to a close a legal saga that began on April 2, 2018, when Jose Medina-Perez left the Newton District Court through a rear courthouse exit all while an ICE officer was waiting in the lobby to take him into custody. The Supreme Judicial Court's ruling centered on a sidebar with Medina-Perez's attorney and the prosecutor during which Joseph instructed her clerk to shut off the courtroom's recording system. "The respondent's statements during that conversation, including her proposal to detain Medina-Perez overnight in State custody, and her conduct in instructing the clerk to turn off the courtroom audio recording system, created an appearance of impropriety in violation of her duties," according to the Thursday ruling from the Supreme Judicial Court. FORMER WISCONSIN JUDGE HANNAH DUGAN AVOIDS JAIL TIME FOR OBSTRUCTING ARREST OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT The Supreme Judicial Court's reprimand came after a hearing officer for the Commission on Judicial Conduct recommended such an action. However, the high court ruled that Joseph was unaware Medina-Perez's attorney, David Jellinek, had devised a plan to help his client evade ICE by escorting him to the courthouse lockup, where the court officer would release him through a rear sally port exit. The court also found that Joseph neither explicitly nor implicitly approved of that plan. Medina-Perez, of the Dominican Republic, had been in Joseph's courtroom to be arraigned on a fugitive-from-justice charge that originated in Pennsylvania. Joseph found there wasn't enough evidence to tie Medina-Perez to the Pennsylvania warrant, and prosecutor Shannon Jurgens recommended he be released without bail on two drug charges he was facing. FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS Joseph then released Medina-Perez on his own personal recognizance and set a pre-trial conference date for the drug possession case. In April 2019, roughly a year later, Joseph and the court officer who let Medina-Perez out through the back door were indicted on charges of obstruction of justice. That case was dropped in 2022 after Joseph agreed to refer herself to the Commission on Judicial Conduct, the agency that investigates allegations of misconduct by Massachusetts judges. The commission concluded that Joseph "engaged in willful judicial misconduct that brought the judicial office into disrepute, as well as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice and unbecoming a judicial officer." After her federal indictment, Joseph was suspended from the bench and unable to work for three years. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Joseph's attorney, Elizabeth Mulvey, said last year during a commission hearing that the case had been distorted in the media, with many coming to believe that her client "let an illegal immigrant out of the door," according to The Associated Press. In a statement to the AP on Thursday, Mulvey said it has been an "incredibly long and difficult eight years for Judge Joseph." "We are grateful to the hearing officer who undertook this monumental task and pleased that his efforts have shown that this was a baseless federal prosecution from the beginning and solely the work of the defense lawyer involved," Mulvey said in a statement. "Judge Joseph is thankful for everyone who stood by her and looks forward to rejoining her colleagues." Joseph, who remains a judge, was assigned in December to administrative duties in the Boston Municipal Court.

articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics: Hill Insider members can join us today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon offer a special episode for the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, including Bill’s experience as a White House reporter inside the presidential bubble when then-President George W. articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics : Hill Insider members can join us today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon offer a special episode for the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, including Bill’s experience as a White House reporter inside the presidential bubble when then-President George W. Bush was informed of the attacks. ]

DALLAS — They shouldn’t really call it a convention, since it isn’t convening anything. There’s no business being done — at least on stage — at the American Airlines Center.

In the Democrats’ short-lived run at similar midterm events in former President Carter’s era, they were careful not to call them conventions, but rather “ conferences .” A convention, if you care about your party’s power and prestige, is supposed to produce something. It is supposed to be important. Not here. No delegates are voting. No platforms are being debated. No leaders are being selected. It’s just a happening .

The gathering here is the fullest flowering of the pseudo-event; the perfect realization of Daniel Boorstin ’s description of “ synthetic novelty .” It’s like a bigger, better version of CPAC. Even the star-spangled logos for the two events look alike . This is part fundraising blitz and part trade show for right-wing influencers, but mostly an effort to get the national news media to pay even more attention to President Trump than usual — which is saying something given that coverage of him has consumed all other stories like a galaxy-crushing black hole since 2015.

The Republican National Committee hasn’t produced a real party platform for a decade, opting in 2020 to wave a press release in front of reporters’ faces, saying in so many words that it wouldn’t be tricked into adopting policy positions that could be used against its candidates or as a way to highlight future reversals. In 2024, there was something it called a “platform,” but it was itself just a press release repeating Trump’s campaign boilerplate with hard or divisive issues all sidestepped.

At the Democrats’ convention of 2024, the last vestige of actual party work — the official nomination of a presidential candidate — was deemed too risky, so it was done on a glorified Zoom call in advance just to make sure nothing would interfere with the coronation of a nominee who had never won a single delegate.

So, in its own way, this gathering in Dallas is the ideal expression of the hollowed-out political parties of our time. A pseudo-convention for a pseudo-party.

But there is a question on the floor here: What’s a majority worth, anyway?

The president told his supporters here that the opening bid was about $1.3 trillion — roughly the size of Saudi Arabia’s annual gross domestic product — paid out in $5,000 bonuses to every adult citizen of the United States if voters agree to keep Republicans in power in the upcoming midterm elections.

That’s in addition to Vice President Vance ’s soccer mom stimulus that would pay $9,000 to married, stay-at-home parents and a newly unveiled $500 in preelection sweeteners to about a million ObamaCare recipients who are getting squeezed by ballooning insurance prices.

Unlike the Vance payments or the ObamaCare booster, which can be done by creative accounting under existing laws, the president’s self-titled “Trump Dividend” is pie in the sky. It’s not impossible that an imagined Republican majority next year would authorize an inflation bomb of that magnitude, but it seems extremely unlikely, even in the populistic GOP.

Consumers are already getting crushed by inflation, high interest rates and high prices. Bond traders are punishing Uncle Sam for becoming a fiscal basket case with a $40 trillion debt and not even concepts of a plan for what to do about it. Even the most cynical Republican lawmaker would be able to see how the hangover would be worse than the high — a lesson Democrats learned the hard way in the Biden era.

So, like the tariff bonuses and DOGE dividends Trump has promised voters before, the midterm payola probably falls into the familiar category of “stuff the president says.” But like his decision to try to rescue two struggling Atlantic City casinos by opening a third one , Trump loves to raise the stakes. Trying to pay off voters with money mortgaged against future generations is a little like using his creditors’ cash to bring in Michael Jackson for the grand opening of the Trump Taj Mahal.

But who is the target audience for the dubious dividend? It certainly isn’t conservatives, who are already feeling seasick from a wild fiscal ride with Trump so far. It can’t be progressives and liberals since, even if they liked the idea of Trump’s anarcho-Keynesianism, they wouldn’t believe his promises anyway. The customers Trump is trying to get through the doors of the GOP casino are those who a) think a massive debt-financed stimulus would be good and b) still tend to believe the things the president says.

The share of Americans who believe that Trump keeps his promises slid from a November 2024 high of 51 percent to 38 percent this spring , and given his many failed efforts to declare victory in the Iran war since then, one does not imagine that number has increased.

Are there enough voters who both a) believe Trump will actually deliver on his promise and b) think that it’s a good policy to lift Republicans’ chances to at least avoid a wipeout of the kind they faced in 2018? People do love free money, but the belated introduction of such a wild policy proposal makes it hard to predict. Certainly, Republicans running in suburban districts and states with large numbers of college-educated voters won’t look forward to explaining their thoughts on the debt bomb.

Their best bet will be to say that it’s just Trump being Trump, and not a serious policy proposal — just a little confection whipped up by the president and nothing to really worry about. That would be fitting: pseudo-policy at a pseudo-convention.

North Carolina mailed out ballots last week—60 days before Election Day, as required by state law. Plenty of other states will join them in the coming weeks. articles.title: USA united after 9/11; why unity is now improbable after a seismic event
articles.summary: An analysis of the twenty-five years following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks suggests that five fundamental shifts in media, politics, government trust, and the economy have created a level of national polarization that makes modern unity unlikely.
articles.body:
In the 25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, our nation has undergone a series of tectonic shifts that have dramatically reshaped the political landscape. These five fundamental changes include the rise and entrenchment of social media, a revolution in traditional media, instant partisan blame games, a crisis of trust in government, and the widest economic disparity in three decades.

Together, these factors have fueled extreme polarization and perpetual disunity, casting doubt on whether Americans could unite as we did in the weeks and months after 9/11 if, God forbid, a similar seismic attack were to occur again. A data point that crystallizes the “then versus now” contrast is presidential job approval.

Two Gallup polls conducted between Aug. 24 and Sept. 10, 2001, showed President George W. Bush with an average approval rating of 53 percent . Gallup’s first post-9/11 poll found Bush’s approval rating had zoomed to 86 percent , and its next poll, conducted on Sept. 21-22, showed 90 percent. Moreover, on Oct. 10, 2001, an ABC News poll reported Bush’s job approval at 92 percent — a record-breaking presidential high for both Gallup and ABC News.

Bush’s approval remained in the 80s until March 2002, when it began to decline gradually.

In comparison, President Trump’s current average job approval is 38 percent , fifteen points below President Bush’s pre-9/11 approval. This gap underscores how unlikely national unity is after a monumental crisis or attack, given the five fundamental changes since September 2001.

The most significant change, and a major cause of disunity, is social media.

Today, anyone can be a reporter, creating and spreading unverified information, falsehoods and exaggerations. Moreover, social media engagement has surpassed traditional news consumption, to the point that many influencers have more followers than the audiences of broadcast and cable channels.

This media transformation is a mirror shattered into thousands of pieces. People learn about news through their own jagged piece, because we now live largely within information silos, receiving information filtered by self-selection that aligns with our political, cultural or economic standing.

Unfortunately, vastly different interpretations of the same event go viral. As a result, people believe what they want to believe, or worse, don’t know what to believe, breeding conspiracies that resist the truth.

Worse, social media fosters numerous us-versus-them mentalities, making it nearly impossible for even a catastrophic event to unite Americans.

Meanwhile, since 9/11, traditional media has been radically diminished, with cable news filtered through its “brand” of what its cultivated audience wants to hear and is accustomed to hearing. Watch how a President Trump-related news story is reported on MS Now compared to Fox News or Newsmax; that bipolar coverage is why disunity is America’s identity.

This disunity has led to the current blame game. When a significant event occurs, officials in both parties seek a partisan spin, amplified by their social and media allies. In this age of hyperpolarization, the president is blamed immediately, while leaders in the president’s party deflect with repetitive identical talking points. January’s Minneapolis ICE shootings are a recent example of instant blame and then the backlash.

In today’s blame-game environment, imagine how differently 9/11 would have been covered. Back then, Americans rallied around the president; today, I would fear a full-scale blame game, exacerbated by a crisis of trust in government.

This trust crisis is documented in a new study: According to the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research , six adults in 10 now have “low trust” in information they receive from the federal government. Imagine how such a lack of trust in government would complicate and hinder national unity during a 9/11-scale attack or similar crisis.

For example, trust issues are dogging the Iran war. The Pentagon is accused of withholding detrimental information about casualties, damage to U.S. Middle East bases, weapons shortfalls, and the true costs of war from Congress and the public.

Our democracy depends on the public trusting our leaders and government, especially during perilous times. Now that trust has diminished, problematic consequences follow.

Finally, economic disparity is the widest in three decades. Data from the Federal Reserve confirms what we see: The rich are getting richer, and the poor are getting poorer. The prevailing consensus is that the American Dream is increasingly out of reach. Although wealth disparity is not new, it has become more pronounced. Would Americans unify during a 9/11-type crisis, when record numbers are struggling daily to make ends meet amid glaring wealth? Let’s hope the answer remains unknown.

Today, as America remembers the shocking deaths, heroism, and unity felt by all on Sept. 11, 2001, we are a different nation. Fortunately, the post- 9/11 anti-terrorism guardrails have held, and we pray they continue. Yet, the fundamental changes in our media, politics, government and economy are not conducive to national unity.

However, this is America, where hope springs eternal and anything is possible. As proof, 25 years later, lower Manhattan is thriving after rising from the ashes.

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill.

articles.title: DeSantis knocks Trump’s $5K dividend payment pledge: ‘More debt and more inflation’
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Thursday criticized President Trump’s controversial proposal to pay out $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if Republicans win the midterms. “What I would say is, if you are getting surplus revenue, you should cut people’s tax and return it to the people,” DeSantis said during a press conference in…
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Thursday criticized President Trump’s controversial proposal to pay out $5,000 checks to every U.S. adult if Republicans win the midterms.

“What I would say is, if you are getting surplus revenue, you should cut people’s tax and return it to the people,” DeSantis said during a press conference in Miami on Thursday.

“What I don’t think you want to do is borrow another trillion-and-a-half dollars and then just try to flood that into the economy, because that will lead to more inflation,” DeSantis continued. “That will lead to more debt and more inflation.”

The governor noted the rising national debt and criticized Congress for not doing more to reach a balanced budget.

“The way it works now in Congress, their incentives are to add debt for short-term political benefit,” DeSantis said. “They never have to make tough decisions.”

The GOP governor, who challenged Trump for the Republican nomination in the 2024 presidential race, has had a tumultuous relationship with the president during his second term, splitting with him on key issues like artificial intelligence regulation.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The president proposed the $5,000 “ Trump dividends ” during a speech at the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday.

The two-day event aimed to drum up excitement among Republican Party voters ahead of the November elections, in which the party is fighting to maintain control over both legislative chambers.

“Here is my promise: If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said during his Wednesday remarks.

The White House did not provide details about how this plan would work, including the potential source of the money, when reached for comment by The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation.

“President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong, drawing a clear contrast with the Democrats’ record of historic inflation, unfettered illegal immigration, skyrocketing crime, and weakness on the world stage,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NewsNation in a statement. “With the continued support of the American people, President Trump will keep delivering real results.”

articles.body: Las próximas elecciones generales se celebrarán a lo largo del año 2027, un momento en el que los españoles van a decidir si Pedro Sánchez deja de ser presidente y si el cambio será para un gobierno del PP, de Vox o de una coalición de ambos partidos. Pero en la izquierda española se quieren poner los cimientos sobre los que tratar de conseguir el poder del Estado o de, al menos, generar los votos suficientes como para que con sus escaños, se pueda conseguir una coalición de la izquierda. En esta situación se encuentra Podemos, que entra ahora en una fase de precampaña electoral donde ya se conoce a la candidata a las elecciones. Ella será Irene Montero, que ya fue ministra de Igualdad en el ejecutivo anterior. Una situación que van a representar hoy mismo los del partido morado con un mitin en Madrid en lo que denominan el arranque de la precampaña de 2027 y en la que Montero, será la líder del partido. Con este liderazgo por parte de Montero, la política que actualmente está ejerciendo funciones en el parlamento europeo, se pone al frente de una “candidatura nítidamente de izquierdas”, aunque no destaca a otras formaciones que se quieran sumar a la lista para que sea lo más amplia posible, lo que significa no cerrar la puerta a todos los que están dentro de Sumar. Apenas han pasado unos días desde que Podemos ha empezado a lanzar un nuevo eslogan que con tres palabras puede dejar a las claras cuáles serán sus argumentos electorales. “Paz, casa y trabajo”, parece que serán sus líneas para seguir de cara a la futura campaña electoral. Según apuntan desde fuentes internas del partido, Montero va a basar su estrategia en una “vuelta a lo básico”, “precios justos para la vivienda”, “trabajar menos para vivir mejor”, “bajar el coste de la vida”, “paz” y “solo hay una vida y un planeta”. Sí que se conoce una de las propuestas de esta candidata, la de una jornada semanal de 35 horas semanales y la de un salario mínimo de 1.800 euros al mes, a su vez que reducir el gasto en defensa

articles.title: Indiana Supreme Court rules for state senator over Trump-backed candidate in GOP primary recount
articles.summary: Indiana’s Supreme Court ruled after a monthslong recount that a Republican state senator narrowly defeated his Trump-backed challenger in the GOP primary for the state Senate seat.
articles.body: Indiana’s Supreme Court on Thursday ruled after a monthslong recount that a Republican state senator narrowly defeated his Trump-backed challenger in the GOP primary for the state Senate seat. The court declared state Sen. Spencer Deery the winner of the Senate District 23 Republican primary in May, certifying that he beat challenger Paula Copenhaver by three votes and ordering that his name appear on the general election ballot in November. The court said Deery secured 6,335 votes to Copenhaver’s 6,332. In the order, Chief Justice Loretta Rush said the court would issue a written opinion further explaining its reasons at a later date. Deery, who has served in the state Senate since 2022, was among the Republican state senators who voted down a redrawn congressional map in Indiana in 2025 that President Donald Trump supported as part of a broader mid-decade redistricting push across the nation. The GOP senators faced primary challengers earlier this year, and several of the incumbents lost, while Deery led Copenhaver by three votes, which she challenged. Trump backed Copenhaver, an aide to Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith and chair of the Fountain County Republican Party. The recount in the race had put Copenhaver in the lead in early August after the Indiana Recount Commission threw out 10 votes mainly for technical reasons involving missing election official signatures on some ballots, the Indiana Capital Chronicle reported at the time, giving Copenhaver a three-vote lead. Deery said Thursday in a post on X that he was pleased by the court’s ruling. “We could never have secure elections in our state if our votes could be invalidated by government error or malfeasance,” he wrote. “Instead, in Indiana, we have set a precedent that says if you do everything right, your right to vote is sacred and protected.” Copenhaver’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Rush said Thursday, however, that a majority of Indiana’s Supreme Court set aside the commission’s final determination that Copenhaver had received the higher number of votes. In the general election, Deery faces West Lafayette City Council member David Sanders, a Democrat, and independent Joshua Brant.

articles.title: FBI agent died of cancer after 9/11 Pentagon response. His widow tells his story.
articles.summary: An FBI agent who responded to the Pentagon on 9/11 later died from cancer. His wife is telling their story.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — When American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon’s western facade at 9:37 a.m. on Sept. 11, 2001, FBI agent Jack Hess rushed to the scene. His wife, Sandy Hess, also an FBI agent at the time, ran to pick up their 1-year-old son from daycare — and was pregnant with their second child. “If you were married in the bureau and had kids and needed to get to those kids, one person would respond to the Pentagon, and the other person went home,” she told NBC News in an interview this week. “He was a supervisor on a terrorism squad. He went, and I don’t think he would have wanted it any other way.” In the aftermath, Jack’s role was to secure evidence for the FBI’s investigation into the attacks. He was one of about 4,000 FBI employees who responded to the crash sites in Virginia, New York and Pennsylvania. While he only spent a matter of hours in direct contact with the hazardous debris in Arlington, he would later be diagnosed with Stage 4 kidney cancer, an illness classified as “caused” by his exposure at the Pentagon, according to the certification process determined by the World Trade Center Health Program. He died of the disease in 2023, at just 64 years old. On Sept. 11, 2001, 2,977 people died in the collapse of the twin towers, at the Pentagon or on United Flight 93, which crashed in a Pennsylvania field. But scores of others who worked in the wreckage have died from illnesses in the years since. At the FBI, more than 400 people have 9/11-related illnesses and at least 33 have died from 9/11-related cancers, according to the bureau. Sandy and Jack Hess met early on in their careers at the FBI and worked together for years, with Jack focused on counterterrorism after the attacks. Jack retired from the bureau in 2009 to pursue a career in the private sector and often thought about what he saw at the Pentagon that day, according to his wife, but never worried his health might be at risk. In 2017, what started as a backache became an emergency trip to the hospital, where a doctor found a tumor on his kidney. Sandy was in disbelief. “I thought, ‘Oh, my gosh, what?’ Like, this is a guy who’s never been sick a day in his life,” she said. Her sit-down with NBC News was the first time she shared their story publicly. When the doctor asked about Jack’s work history, she recalled saying: “‘Wait, my husband responded to the Pentagon.’ And she looked at me and she said, ‘There has been a huge increase in kidney cancer since 9/11.’” “Nobody had any kind of protection on. We didn’t even think about it. I mean, it was an emergency situation. We had a mission,” Sandy said. “And people ask all the time if Jack knew he was going to get this cancer, maybe he wouldn’t have gone that day. And I said, ‘You’re absolutely wrong. He would have done it, and he would have been proud, and we’re proud of him. He’s a hero.’” In 2019, the FBI created a video in which first responders like Jack encouraged others to sign up for health benefits and receive proper medical screenings. In it, Jack said: “It was 17 years ago. I’m fine. I was there for one day. I’m fine. In reality, those were bad assumptions.” Jack grew increasingly concerned that the effects of that day could threaten the health of his colleagues, even many years later, his wife said. “Don’t be afraid to go out and get screened and find that something’s wrong with you, whether it’s related to 9/11 or not. Seventeen years is not too long. Eighteen or 19 years probably won’t be too long. You can still get sick from this,” Jack said at the time. Four years after that plea, he died, surrounded by his wife and four children, who are hoping to carry on his message to others. “We are not being proactive enough. We just aren’t. People who have responded to 9/11, they need yearly scans,” Sandy said. “Some of this could have been avoided had a scan been done, and maybe, maybe he would have had Stage 2 cancer … but why does he have to wait for a death sentence?” Specifically, Sandy said that more thorough CT scans — imaging tests that show detailed pictures of the human body — could lead to earlier diagnoses, as opposed to the yearly physicals covered by the FBI. The FBI, for its part, says it continues to encourage first responders to register for the World Trade Center benefits screening program. As for how she would like him to be remembered, Sandy said her husband “left a legacy of courage, determination and selflessness.” Now, a quarter of a century after the attacks, it’s not just Sept. 11 that marks a difficult date on the calendar. “Every holiday is hard. There’s always, always an open seat everywhere you go, so it’s really hard. Father’s Day, the toughest holiday there is. But I try to tell the kids to reflect on all the good times we’ve had and appreciate the time we had with Jack. I had a great marriage for 25 years. Many people don’t have that,” she said. “He was a father that was hands-on, involved with his kids, and many kids don’t have that, either. And so I try to teach my kids to appreciate what we have, not what we lost.”

articles.title: SEAL who killed bin Laden recalls 9/11 moment that changed his life: ‘Welcome to my world’
articles.summary: Rob O'Neill recalls watching the World Trade Center attacks from a German operations center, where Osama bin Laden and al Qaeda were first named.
articles.body: Rob O’Neill, the Navy SEAL credited with killing Usama bin Laden, had just returned from a 40-day deployment to Kosovo when the world changed forever. The former Navy SEAL told Fox News Digital in an interview ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 that he was stationed in Stuttgart, Germany, on Sept. 11, 2001, preparing equipment and catching up on emails when every television channel switched to breaking news. "At first, there was a hole in the North Tower," O’Neill recalled. "No one even knew what the North Tower of the World Trade Center was that day." O’Neill and his fellow service members initially wondered whether a small plane had accidentally crashed into the building. But after the second plane struck the South Tower shortly after 9 a.m. Eastern time, they immediately understood the significance of what they were watching. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS "I’m in an operations center with intel analysts and Navy SEALs, and we all collectively knew that our lives just changed," O’Neill said. The names of Usama bin Laden and al Qaeda were soon mentioned in the room. "We’re on a deployment to Germany, we’re probably going to Sudan. We don’t know where," he said. "The name Usama bin Laden was said in that room, al Qaeda. And we just knew our lives were going to change." O’Neill eventually re-enlisted in the Navy in the aftermath of the attacks and went on to serve with SEAL Team Six, the elite special operations unit that ultimately carried out the raid that killed bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011. But in the immediate aftermath of 9/11, he did not know he would play a role in hunting down the mastermind of the attacks. "I knew, for me, the Navy was never going to be a career," O’Neill said. "I joined because I thought it was cool, re-enlisted because of the guys, re-enlisted because of 9/11, go to SEAL Team Six." As the reality of the attacks set in, O’Neill briefly left the secure operations area and called his brother in Montana, who worked in morning radio. AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET "I said, ‘Hey man, I don’t know if you’re up. Turn the TV on,’" O’Neill recalled. "He said, ‘Which channel?’ I said, ‘Doesn’t matter.’ And then he turned it on and all I said to him was, ‘Welcome to my world.’" Looking back on the 25 years that have passed since the tragedy that took the lives of 2,977 people, O’Neill says he was moved by the way the country came together after the terrorist attacks and while he hopes there is never another 9/11, he does wish Americans could recapture the spirit of unity that followed. He recalled the image of lawmakers from both parties standing together on the steps of the Capitol and singing "God Bless America." "It was about America first, not foreign interests," O’Neill said. "It was a time of unity." Roughly a third of the U.S. population was not alive on 9/11 and O’Neill told Fox News Digital what his message for them about the tragedy would be. "No matter what, at night, don’t go to bed angry with anyone in your family," he said. "Hug everyone that’s there and tell them you love them." "You remember on Monday, September 10, some people didn’t do that, and they were jumping out of skyscrapers the next day," O’Neill said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He urged Americans to focus on their families, neighbors, communities and first responders. "If you can take care of each other, and you master those basics, then the world around you is going to be fine," he said. "Sometimes it’s better just to put the phone down and go outside and look at the sun." O’Neill said that spending time outside can provide perspective in an increasingly chaotic world. "You’ll know that you’re not random," he said. "You’re here by design. God loves you. He puts you here on purpose." O’Neill said the legacy of the attacks and his path from Butte, Montana to the elite SEAL Team 6 is a reminder of the opportunities available to Americans, particularly young people. "If you want to do something, leave the house," O’Neill said. "You can do anything you want." "Don’t let the negativity get to you," he added. "At any moment you decide, you can do that."

articles.title: Giuliani blasts Mamdani’s 9/11 toxic air blame as buried city records come to light
articles.summary: Rudy Giuliani's spokesperson accuses Mayor Zohran Mamdani of scoring political points after 170,000 pages of 9/11 toxic air records were released.
articles.body: Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani's team is firing back at Mayor Zohran Mamdani after Mamdani accused past city officials of misleading New Yorkers about toxic air following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Giuliani spokesperson Ted Goodman accused Mamdani of seeking to "score cheap partisan political points" by directing blame toward local officials who rushed to the scene of the attacks while overlooking the radical Islamic terrorists responsible for killing nearly 3,000 people. "Now would be a good time to remind Mayor Mamdani that cowardly terrorists acting in the name of Islam are 100 percent responsible for all of the death and destruction on September 11, 2001, and for all of the suffering and illness that have continued since that day," Goodman said in a statement to Fox News Digital. MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?' The records released by Mamdani’s administration include more than 170,000 pages documenting the city’s response to the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath. The initial release includes 68 boxes of records from the Department of Environmental Protection that were not located until 2025, and records related to 7 World Trade Center. The records include documents from Giuliani’s administration, including a memo sent to Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that warned the city faced potentially multimillion-dollar lawsuits from New Yorkers who claimed health advisories failed to protect them from toxic exposure and that the sites were inadequately cleaned up. MAMDANI UNDER FIRE AFTER SYMBOLIC 9/11 PEN GOES TO FORMER AL QAEDA DEFENSE LAWYER At a news conference announcing the release, Mamdani said the documents showed that officials across multiple administrations had information about hazardous conditions but failed to adequately inform the public. "I wish there was a limited number of people who misled the public that I could describe them in just a few names," Mamdani said during a Tuesday news conference. "But the truth is that, as we have heard, this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted, and we are here to release these documents today because, for a long time, New Yorkers have known the truth, and yet they have been unable to see the truth in any document that's been presented to them." Mamdani said the release was intended to give New Yorkers access to records that had been difficult to obtain for years. His administration said the city had settled two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch as part of the release and created a public portal containing the documents. "People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air. And then, when they began to contend with the symptoms of the illnesses that followed, the government that had not hesitated to send them into harm's way was nowhere to be found," Mamdani said. NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS Thousands of first responders, residents, workers and others exposed to the World Trade Center site have since developed illnesses recognized by the World Trade Center Health Program as related to 9/11 exposure. The program continues to provide treatment and monitoring for people suffering from certified 9/11-related conditions. Former Republican New York Gov. George Pataki, who was governor at the time of the attacks, said in an interview with the New York Post this week that he had been diagnosed with restrictive airway disease, which he attributed to his exposure to toxins at Ground Zero. The newly released records provide additional detail about environmental hazards found in the years after the attacks, including asbestos detected at 15 John Street in Lower Manhattan. The records document asbestos findings at multiple locations and provide additional detail about the city’s environmental response. The records show that asbestos was detected at some locations at levels below applicable cleanup or exposure benchmarks and at others at levels that appeared to exceed them. Health authorities have said there is no known safe level of asbestos exposure. Then-EPA Administrator Christie Todd Whitman said in a Sept. 18, 2001, press release that air monitoring results indicated the air near the World Trade Center was safe to breathe, days after the EPA first issued assurances about environmental hazards on Sept. 13. MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY Goodman pointed to the federal government’s role in communicating about air quality after the attacks, noting that the EPA issued public assurances about conditions near Ground Zero. An EPA Inspector General review later concluded that the data available at the time did not fully support the agency’s broad assurances about air safety. "The EPA, a federal agency, issued press releases and public statements declaring that air samples showed the air quality near Ground Zero was safe," Goodman said, referring to Giuliani's response. "The agency later apologized for those statements, saying it did the best it could with the knowledge available at the time." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Whitman later apologized for the assurances in a 2016 interview, saying she was sorry for people who became sick or died and that she and the EPA had done the best they could with the information available at the time. The release of the documents follows a petition with more than 100,000 signatures from 9/11 victims' family members requesting that Mamdani not attend the memorial ceremony at Ground Zero Friday. "This mayor is not serving us," Charles Wolf, who lost his wife on 9/11, said at a noon news conference. "He's serving himself. We are asking respectfully that he not show up." "Even though there is going to be other politicians there, these are the politicians that helped us push beneficial laws through and literally held our hand during that time," Wolf continued. "Mayor Mamdani has not shown any of that, none of it. He just wants to be there because he wants to be there." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The mayor’s office said the initial release represents only the beginning of the city’s effort to make its 9/11 records publicly accessible, with additional documents expected to be added to the portal. articles.title: Trump admin’s fraud crackdown targets foreigners accused of infiltrating US federal programs
articles.summary: The FBI's Most Wanted list names Onur Simsek, a Turkish national accused of a defense procurement fraud scheme involving fake parts for U.S. military gear.
articles.body: The Trump administration is intensifying its efforts to target foreign nationals accused of defrauding the U.S. government, as the FBI and other federal agencies pursue suspects operating from overseas. Last week, the FBI released a "Most Wanted" list highlighting alleged fraud suspects as the administration continues its broader crackdown on fraud. Officials say the involvement of foreign nationals in multiple schemes has heightened concerns about overseas actors exploiting U.S. government programs. Among those named is Onur Simsek, a Turkish national whom the FBI believes is living in Turkey. Prosecutors accuse Simsek of leading a defense procurement fraud scheme that secured U.S. military contracts by falsely certifying Turkish-made parts as tested and qualified, potentially rendering critical military equipment inoperable. FBI LAUNCHES 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AS DOJ CHARGES OHIO DEFENDANTS IN $30M MEDICAID SCHEME FOR KIDS Federal authorities allege Simsek is one of a number of foreign nationals who have infiltrated and exploited U.S. federal funds to obtain taxpayer funds. In a statement, General Services Administration Administrator Ed Forst pointed to Simsek's alleged conduct while discussing the administration's efforts to combat fraud. "Simsek's alleged procurement fraud deprived taxpayers of value, denied honest businesses fair opportunity, and diverted critical resources from American warfighters," Forst said. "Under President Trump and Vice President Vance, GSA will continue working relentlessly to identify and hold accountable those who try to cheat the federal marketplace and steal from the American people." The General Services Administration Office of Inspector General has assisted in the investigation, according to the agency. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD Foreign nationals have become a focus of the administration's broader fraud investigations, including scrutiny of an alleged Medicaid and child care fraud scheme involving members of Minnesota's Somali community that sparked clashes between federal agents and protesters earlier this year. In an interview with Fox News Digital last month, Vice President JD Vance said authorities have observed what he described as a "clear pattern" in some fraud cases involving immigrant communities. "You definitely see patterns in certain communities," Vance said. "It'll start as maybe one Somali person takes advantage of the system, or realizes you don't even have to have children to get money from these programs. You could just claim that you have children, there's no verification. Then, word spreads like wildfire, and that program gets tapped into by the same members of that community." EXCLUSIVE: FBI ADDS ALLEGED COVID FRAUDSTER ACCUSED OF TAKING $5M FROM KIDS' MEAL PROGRAM TO MOST WANTED LIST According to the Justice Department, Simsek and his co-conspirators used a U.S.-based front company between April 2019 and February 2022 to obtain contracts to supply parts for Navy submarines, Marine Corps armored vehicles, Army M-60 tanks and other military equipment. Prosecutors allege the parts were manufactured in Turkey, then repackaged to conceal their country of origin before being sold to the U.S. government. The "War Dogs" -style scheme was also allegedly in collaboration with Yuksel Senbol, who was sentenced to prison for conspiracy to defraud in 2024. An arrest warrant for Simsek was ordered in Tampa, Florida in October 2023. The FBI is offering a reward of up to $150,000 for information leading to Simsek's arrest and conviction. WHITE HOUSE EXPOSES ‘TRANSSHIPMENT SCAM’ COSTING US UP TO $26B, POINTS FINGER AT CHINA In late July, the FBI arrested Khalid Ahmed Satary, who FBI Director Kash Patel said participated in a conspiracy that fraudulently billed Medicare more than $547 million for medically unnecessary genetic tests between 2016 and 2019. articles.title: ‘Trump-level’ smackdown earns Vance roaring praise as 2028 buzz builds at GOP convention
articles.summary: JD Vance fired back at a protester waving a Mexican flag during his RNC convention speech in Dallas, offering to buy them a plane ticket to Mexico.
articles.body: Republicans reached a consensus that Vice President JD Vance solidified his position as the presumptive 2028 presidential candidate with his "Trump-level" smackdown of a foreign flag-waving protester who disrupted his speech at the Republican National Convention. Vance did not hesitate after a protester interrupted his primetime speech in Dallas on Thursday by waving the flags of the Palestinian Authority and Mexico. He recalled to those watching his speech on TV: "What the people at home missed is that we just had a protester interrupting us and waving the Mexican flag." "Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your a-- over there. I'll buy you the plane ticket," the VP said, to which the crowd erupted into applause. "JD Vance just MIC DROPPED a leftist heckler who interrupted him waving a Mexican flag...this place is DEAFENING," conservative commentator Eric Daugherty wrote on X, adding, "TOTAL PANDEMONIUM." CROWD ERUPTS AS VANCE SMACKS DOWN PROTESTER WAVING MEXICAN FLAG: 'GET YOUR A-- OVER THERE' Popular conservative pundit Benny Johnson called Vance’s quick wit an "epic response." President Donald Trump supporter and activist Scott Pressler similarly praised Vance for reacting "without missing a beat," and called it "an iconic moment." "This was masterful. A Trump-level move from JD Vance," wrote Overton, a conservative commentary and news account. "Vice President Vance perfectly handled a protestor waving a Mexican flag at the RNC in Dallas. Then he fired back with a savage one-liner that sent the American Airlines Center into absolute bedlam." The moment was capped off with a "USA!" chant from those in the crowd at the GOP Midterm Convention. Students for Trump co-founder Ryan Fournier wrote, "JD Vance just absolute [sic] WIPED THE FLOOR with a leftist heckler who interrupted his rally waving a Mexican flag." "The crowd went completely WILD. Unbelievable energy," wrote Fournier. VANCE DECLARES DEMOCRATS ‘PARTY OF HATRED,’ SAYS PARTY HAS MOVED BEYOND BIG GOVERNMENT, CENSORSHIP "JD Vance just notched the most iconic moment of the RNC when he told a protester waving a Mexican flag exactly what all red blooded Americans were thinking," wrote Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet. Commentator Brilyn Hollyhand put it simply, posting on X, "Yea JD for President after this." Vance recovered from the interruption quickly, telling the crowd, "Ladies and gentlemen, I had a whole speech written. But I think I’ve got to change it because we just discovered the symbol of the far left — an idiot waving … a Mexican flag at a protest when he should be waving the flag of the United States of America." "Now, we all know, of course, that as much as that person might wave around a foreign flag, he'd much rather live in Dallas, or in Cincinnati, or in any one of our great cities than Mexico," President Donald Trump's No. 2 continued. "But while we wave the American flag and fight for the American dream, we have to remind ourselves tonight that the good life that is the foundation of this country's promise is not guaranteed." CHARLIE KIRK HONORED AT GOP CONVENTION WITH CALL TO REJECT ‘COMFORTABLE LOSING’ "Every generation of Americans has had to fight for these things when it's our turn," he went on. "And this fall, the Democrats are running candidates who will tell your children what they're allowed to say, how they're allowed to live, and importantly, who they ought to hate, because that's what the Democrat Party is about in 2026," Vance continued. "It's not about you, it's about foreign fraudsters, and it's about who they hate. And we got to send their a--es back in November." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Speculation has swirled over who will be the heir to Trump's MAGA throne in 2028. The consensus so far among Republicans appears to be split between Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio — but a lot could change before the next presidential election.

articles.title: Top House chairman warns Congress against 'complacency' 25 years after 9/11
articles.summary: House Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino warns Congress must stop being reactive to prevent another World Trade Center attack.
articles.body: House Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., remembers exactly where he was when the World Trade Center was attacked on Sept. 11, 2001. "I was a senior in high school. I was in Mr. Ponzi's government class. And that's when the first plane hit. And one of the other teachers came in and was telling Mr. Ponzi about it," he told Fox News Digital. "We all thought it was a little plane. And then we went to the next class. And then the second plane hit, and everybody realized that stuff was wrong." Twenty-five years later, Garbarino leads a congressional committee that oversees a Cabinet department created explicitly after the terror attack. He's warning that Congress needs to change how it deals with potential threats to avoid another tragedy of that scale. "Being chairman of the committee, being a New Yorker, it's one of those things you focus on, and you want to make sure another 9/11 doesn't happen, and doesn't ever happen again. And that's my goal. That's my priority," he said. 9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS "Congress is very good at being reactive... We don't want another 9/11. So if I could leave my fingerprints on something here, it's the fact that the focus, Congress' focus on national security, Congress' focus on homeland security or safety, is that we address an issue before something happens." HOW 9/11 TRANSFORMED SYNAGOGUE SECURITY INTO A NEW REALITY FOR THE JEWISH COMMUNITY He said Congress needed to get into the habit of passing laws ahead of time, "instead of being like, 'Oh my God I can't believe this happened, how did this happen, let's fix it now.'" "That's why 9/11 happened. 9/11 happened because our intelligence agencies, they were siloed, they were not sharing information. I don't know if it was a complacency or whatever, but there were a lot of problems," Garbarino said. "I don't want to fall into that same complacency." Garbarino represents New York's 2nd Congressional District, part of Long Island's south shore. As a suburb of New York City, its residents are deeply attuned to that tragedy 25 years ago. "We have people that lost loved ones that day that are still dealing with it 25 years later," Garbarino said. "So the scar is still there." His district and others are also still dealing with illnesses stemming from that day, including first responders who bravely rushed to the collapsing twin towers. "There are now more people that have died from 9/11-related illnesses than died on the actual day. So it's a day that keeps taking people away from us," Garbarino said. "You have firemen who, 9/11 was their first call. They were 21, 22 years old. They're now 47... And a lot of these, some of these cancers, they take a while to take hold, and they're now just getting sick." SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING Earlier this year, President Donald Trump signed legislation led by Garbarino and others to address a projected funding shortfall for the World Trade Center Health Program, which helps survivors pay for their medical treatment. He said nearly all congressional districts across the country have at least one person participating in the program, a testament to how widespread the tragedy's effects are. So this does affect the entire country," Garbarino said.

articles.title: ‘Their souls are in that steel’: 9/11 beam makes emotional stop in Indianapolis before return to NYC
articles.summary: A 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center's South Tower arrived at the Indiana War Memorial as part of Tunnel to Towers' nationwide tour.
articles.body: A 21-foot, 16,900-pound steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center’s South Tower arrived in Indianapolis last month as part of a nationwide tour commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in a tribute that will ultimately end up back at Ground Zero. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation brought its "Steel Across America" tour to the Indiana War Memorial and Museum on Aug. 19, marking the tour’s 31st stop. The beam is traveling more than 10,500 miles through 21 states and Washington, D.C., before returning to New York City for a Sept. 11 commemoration. The piece of steel recovered from Ground Zero in the days after the attacks by first responders who rushed to the site has since become a symbol of the nearly 3,000 civilians, firefighters, police officers, emergency workers and military personnel who died that day. "For the past four months, communities across the country have welcomed this sacred piece of American history with incredible emotion," Tunnel to Towers Chairman and CEO Frank Siller said in a press release. "Watching people stand in front of that steel, hugging it, praying over it, weeping, reminds me every single day of why we do this work." TUNNEL TO TOWERS ANNOUNCES 'STEEL ACROSS AMERICA' TOUR TO MARK 25 YEARS SINCE 9/11 ATTACKS The Indianapolis ceremony included a color guard, a pipes and drums procession, the national anthem performed by the Voices of the Indianapolis Fire Department and an invocation from Indianapolis Fire Department Chaplain Mike Gatliff. Indianapolis Fire Division Chief Tom Neal and Timothy Winslow, a retired major general and executive director of the Indiana War Memorial and Museum, also addressed the crowd about the connection between the city’s first responders, veterans and the legacy of 9/11. FIRST RESPONDERS HONOR WORLD TRADE CENTER BEAM ARRIVING AT BOSTON FALLEN HEROES MEMORIAL "Bringing this steel to Indianapolis, and to a museum that has stood for over a century as a tribute to American sacrifice, is deeply moving," FDNY Lt. Jack Kielty, a Tunnel to Towers board member, said. "Indiana veterans and first responders understand what it means to serve." The event also highlighted Indiana’s own connection to the attacks. Nine Hoosiers died on Sept. 11, while Indianapolis Task Force One sent rescuers to Ground Zero. Six members of the team later died from illnesses linked to their work in the toxic environment, according to the Indiana War Memorial. Scott Nokes, a Marine Corps veteran and Tunnel to Towers recipient, spoke to attendees about the significance of allowing people to see the steel in person. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Out of the 2,977 lives that were lost, there’s over 1,000 bodies that were never recovered specifically from Ground Zero in New York," Nokes said. "Their souls are in that steel, and if you touch it, you feel it." The foundation’s tour is designed in part to connect younger Americans with an event that many were too young to remember or were not alive to witness. Nokes said seeing the artifact firsthand offers a connection that cannot be replicated by books or documentaries. The Indianapolis stop was followed by an appearance at the Cincinnati Fire Museum. The tour’s final stops include West Point, Boston and Washington, D.C., before the steel returns to New York City. When the steel returns to New York City on Sept. 11, Frank Siller and members of the Siller family will carry it through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel, retracing the route Stephen Siller took 25 years earlier after strapping 60 pounds of gear to his back and running toward the World Trade Center. The steel will accompany the procession through the tunnel but will not enter or stop at the World Trade Center site.

articles.title: 'Feels like yesterday': 9/11 victim's daughter says families still fighting for justice 25 years later
articles.summary: Angela Mistrulli and 9/11 families are pressing Congress at the Republican convention to fund the USVSST Fund before a critical Sept. 30 deadline.
articles.body: DALLAS - Twenty-five years after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Angela Mistrulli said, "It feels like forever, but it also feels like yesterday." Mistrulli, whose father was killed in the collapse of the World Trade Center twin towers in New York City, is the founder of American Victims of State-Sponsored Terrorism (AVSSTU), which represents victims and families impacted by terrorist attacks. She spoke with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention, where she and other 9/11 family members, Gold Star families, and families of civilian victims were pressing to meet with political leaders on an urgent mission as the clock ticked towards a critical deadline. BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER "Congress created the United States Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund (USVSST Fund). It was supposed to be a place for all victims to be able to go and receive some sort of relief. It was a lifeline to over 22,000 victims," Mistrulli explained. "Unfortunately, that fund has run dry, and September 30th is the fiscal deadline for Congress to act in order for victims to receive relief." Established in 2015, the USVSST Fund has provided over $10 billion to victims harmed by international state-sponsored terrorism, including personal representatives for those who lost their lives from acts of terrorism such as the 9/11 attacks. Mistrulli emphasized that 25 years after the 9/11 attacks, "We are still fighting for justice, transparency, recognition, and relief that Congress promised us." "We're here not only to memorialize the 25th anniversary of 9/11, but also to try to get some face time with these leaders and these higher ups to be able to discuss this urgent and critical topic," she added. 9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD' With the fiscal-year cutoff approaching Sept. 30, Congress would need to authorize additional funding for victims holding unpaid terrorism judgments to be paid. A bipartisan group of lawmakers from New York introduced a bill in July that would require the U.S. Department of the Treasury to loan $3 billion annually to the fund for fiscal years 2027, 2028 and 2029. The bill, H.R. 9795, was named after Mistrulli’s father — the Never Forget the Victims of Terrorism: Joseph D. Mistrulli and Alan Kleinberg USVSST Fund Solvency Act. The Department of Justice has acknowledged that available USVSST funds remain insufficient to fully compensate victims' claims that have been and are anticipated to continue to grow. Mistrulli and members of the AVSSTU are at the Republican midterm convention to push to influence members of Congress in voting to authorize continued funding for victims as the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks concludes the week of convention activities in Dallas. GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS "This is a hard one this year. 25 years. It feels like forever, but it also feels like yesterday, and it's also disappointing because I feel like our country has come so far away from who we were on September 12th," Mistrulli said. "It's also exhausting that it's been 25 years of us fighting for justice."
