articles.title: 9/11 sent them to war. 25 years later, veterans grapple with what followed
articles.summary: John Byrnes was at Hunter College on 9/11 before securing Ground Zero. Now he and four other veterans wrestle with what the wars accomplished.
articles.body: John Byrnes was swimming in a pool beneath Hunter College in Manhattan on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he stepped outside for coffee and heard sirens blaring down Lexington Avenue. He learned that a plane had hit the World Trade Center. Minutes later, he saw the North Tower collapse on a campus television and immediately headed toward his National Guard armory. Byrnes spent the next two weeks helping secure Ground Zero. And spent the following years in both Iraq and Afghanistan. Each of the five veterans who spoke with Fox News Digital ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 remembers where they were when they learned the nation had been attacked — and how Sept. 11 changed the trajectory of their life and service. Some were already in uniform. Others, including a successful businessman and a teenager who watched the attacks unfold on television at his school, felt compelled to enlist. Looking back 25 years later, Byrnes draws a sharp distinction between the wars, including the decision to respond to the terrorist attacks and the choices that followed to continue the war on terror. "The decision to go to Afghanistan, that was absolutely necessary," Byrnes, who is now a strategic director at Concerned Veterans for America, told Fox News Digital. "The decision to go to Iraq, which was not necessary." "The decision to stay in Afghanistan for so long was unfortunate, but it all came down to that day." ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE' "The decisions that didn’t seem wrong at the time were just pebble after pebble into an avalanche," he said. Veterans who spoke to Fox News Digital all went to war believing they were protecting Americans by keeping the fight "over there." Twenty-five years later, they remain proud that they answered that call. Their harder questions are about what came afterward: how the mission expanded, what two decades of war accomplished and whether the country ultimately made good on the sacrifices it asked of them — and the people of Afghanistan. Chris Hoff was working for the state Department of Corrections while studying to become a special-education teacher in his post-military service life. For him, the decision to return to service came as he watched the towers fall from the New Jersey shoreline. "When September 11th happened, I knew right then and there that I was going back in the military," Hoff told Fox News Digital. He returned to the reserves and deployed to Afghanistan twice. During his second deployment, he suffered multiple concussions and was ultimately forced to end his military career. "For 20 years, all I knew was prison and war," Hoff said. "And I was good at both of them." When he could no longer continue in either career, Hoff said he felt as though he had failed. But he credits connecting with the Wounded Warrior Project and beginning equine therapy for ultimately saving his life. Hoff now shares his story in hopes other veterans will seek help sooner. "If I can help just one soldier... get help," he said, "it’s okay to get help. It truly is. I’m glad I did." If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Rep. Troy Downing, R-Mont., now serving his first term in Congress, was moose hunting in remote Alaska when he first learned that the World Trade Center had been attacked. He had been dropped in the bush with only an aviation radio, and no planes had flown overhead for days. When a pilot finally reached the hunting party, Downing learned that both towers had fallen. "This country has been good to me," Downing recalled thinking at the time when learning about the attack on U.S. soil. "What have I ever done to deserve it? We’re being attacked right now. Everything that this country stands for is being attacked. And I’ve never done anything to deserve this." Downing, the son of a single teenage mom, grew up poor. He went on to teach at New York University and help build a technology startup that became Yahoo. He was 34, with no prior military service, when he returned home and walked into a recruiter’s office the next day. Downing joined the Air National Guard and served in combat search and rescue, including during two deployments to Afghanistan. The way the war ended did not change Downing’s view of the decision to serve. But it did shape how he viewed what the country ultimately did with that service. Downing called the withdrawal under former President Joe Biden "a blemish" that "squandered everything that we gained there." He urged veterans not to conclude that their own sacrifices had been in vain. "I just want to make sure that my brothers and sisters in arms, the folks that have served this mission, understand that they served this country and they served honorably," Downing told Fox News Digital. "And not think just because of that one misstep that it was in vain because you stepped up to the dotted line when your country asked you to." MAMDANI TO RELEASE DOCUMENTS ON 9/11 HEALTH IMPACTS BEFORE 25TH ANNIVERSARY Brandon Newberry has wrestled directly with that question. Just 16 years old when he walked out of gym class and saw news coverage of the World Trade Center falling on a TV in his Spanish classroom, Newberry said: "I just felt lost and hopeless." "I wanted to do something," he went on. "I wanted to help. I knew there were people suffering, people dying and it hurt me really bad." Newberry joined the Marine Corps in 2006 because he believed the branch would put him closest to the fight. He deployed to Iraq in 2007 and later served two tours in Afghanistan. "My whole philosophy behind it was take the fight to them," Newberry told Fox News Digital. "As long as I kept it in their backyard, they couldn’t put it in our backyard." Newberry said he spent roughly seven years in Afghanistan, including time as a government contractor after leaving the Marines. The years there gave him a close view of the Afghan people and the changes he believed had taken place while U.S. forces were in the country. "At the time, women were allowed to go to school. We had women doctors," he said. "They didn’t have that fear of the unknown, as long as we were there trying to help them out." Newberry said the U.S. "fumbled the ball" and could have done more to establish a lasting government and security force before leaving. "It could have definitely been done better," he said. He also felt the conclusion of the two-decade war was a tragedy. "The withdrawal hurt us military guys. I lost a lot of good friends, and it hurts." The ending, Newberry said, raised a more personal question about the years he had spent there: "I almost feel like everything that I did was almost for nothing because, again, I feel like at this point I failed the Afghan people." Michael Matthews was already serving in the Army when the attacks happened that fateful day in 2001. He deployed to Iraq in 2003 with one of the first divisions to cross the border from Kuwait. His team was later hit by an IED. Matthews suffered injuries to his face, neck, head, back, arms and legs, spent three and a half weeks in a coma and remained hospitalized for nearly nine months. He had hoped to make a career of military service, but the injuries forced him onto a different path. "It just ultimately changed the trajectory of what my goal was, which was to, of course, do this amazing life in the military and make a huge career out of it," Matthews told Fox News Digital. Instead, Matthews said the experience also gave him a new purpose: "Helping veterans and helping the community." For the men who served, questions about the wars do not necessarily translate into regret over their own decision to fight. Byrnes said one of the central lessons of the post-9/11 wars is that military and political leaders must look beyond the immediate objective — and be willing to acknowledge when a strategy is not working. "You can never admit failure," Byrnes said. "You always want to, no matter how bad things were, set the positive note. You tell the boss you’re winning until somebody else comes to take your place so you can get promoted without saying that you’re not winning." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But 25 years after the attacks, the veterans’ reflections resist a simple judgment on the wars that followed. They describe pride in having served despite the physical and psychological wounds, expressed frustration over the decisions that prolonged or expanded the wars, and issued sharply different conclusions about what the United States ultimately accomplished in its 20-year endeavor in the Middle East. Matthews put that tension simply. "We’re proud of what we did," he said. "Even though we may not have fully understood what we were doing or why we were doing it."

articles.title: Modi again urges Putin to end Ukraine war ahead of BRICS summit
articles.summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to enter negotiations to end the war in Ukraine as the two leaders met i...
articles.body:
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to enter negotiations to end the war in Ukraine ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.

The Indian Foreign Ministry's statement referred to conflicts "in the Black Sea region" as the Ukraine war was on the agenda during the bilateral talks between Modi and Putin.

India, a major buyer of Russian oil and grain, has been affected by difficulties in Black Sea shipping caused by Russian and Ukrainian strikes, with Indian sailors falling victim to drone attacks.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to enter negotiations to end the war in Ukraine as the two leaders met in New Delhi ahead of the BRICS summit.

Dialogue and diplomacy are the right way to resolve conflicts, Modi told Putin, according to a statement from the Indian Foreign Ministry.

India is ready to support peace efforts, he said.

The bilateral talks came ahead of a two-day BRICS summit, beginning on Saturday.

The Ukraine war is on the agenda, with the Indian Foreign Ministry's wording referring to conflicts "in the Black Sea region."

India is a major buyer of Russian oil and grain. It has been affected by difficulties in Black Sea shipping caused by Russian and Ukrainian strikes, with Indian sailors having fallen victim to drone attacks.

New Delhi, which maintains close ties with both Western partners and Moscow, has taken a broadly pragmatic stance on the conflict since the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022.

However, Modi stepped up his rhetoric at a meeting in Kyrgyzstan in late August, urging Putin to end the fighting in front of cameras.

The path from an endless war to the end of the war must be taken, he said. Putin responded that Russia was on that path.

How direct Modi's words were at the latest meeting in New Delhi remained unclear.

Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov confirmed that Ukraine was discussed, the Russian news agency TASS reported.

Indian media did not publish any video of Modi's remarks.

The Indian statement said Modi and Putin agreed to strengthen the special strategic partnership between the two countries.

Cooperation continues to show considerable growth, they said.

articles.title: AOC’s ‘modern-day lynchings’ claim torn to shreds online as Black hanging case findings tell a different story
articles.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ayanna Pressley demand DOJ and FBI investigate Black hanging deaths, alleging racial terror and modern-day lynchings.
articles.body: This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255). Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., warned Friday of "racial terror" and "widespread modern-day lynchings" in the U.S. as she joined dozens of Democrats demanding that the DOJ and FBI investigate hanging deaths of Black Americans. Multiple official findings in several recent cases show that law enforcement or medical examiners ruled the deaths suicides, while at least one very recent death remains under a homicide investigation. AOC alleges there is systemic racial bias at the agencies, while fellow progressive lawmaker Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., called the hangings a "national crisis" in a letter to the agencies that she spearheaded. MS RACHEL SPEAKS OUT ON BLACK HANGING CASES AS RALEIGH DEATH IS DECLARED SUICIDE "This year, there have already been 10 reported hangings of Black people in the U.S. I’ m proud to have signed onto Rep. Pressley’s letter to address these widespread modern-day lynchings and put a stop to this racial terror," Ocasio-Cortez wrote on X in support of the call. Pressley warned in her letter that "Black folks are being found hanged in America" and insisted: "We cannot stand by while strange fruit hangs from trees across the country." The letter, addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, was signed by Pressley, Ocasio-Cortez and about 50 Democrats. They demanded a "thorough, transparent, and comprehensive federal investigation into every hanging death of a Black individual across the United States," arguing that federal agencies have failed for decades to adequately investigate such deaths. FAMILY IDENTIFIES YOUNG WOMAN FOUND FATALLY SHOT IN HOME OWNED BY REP AYANNA PRESSLEY'S HUSBAND One 2026 case involved the death of a 21-year-old Atlanta man who had gone missing. He was later found hanging from a tree in a Cobb County park, where officials ruled out foul play and deemed the death a suicide, according to Atlanta’s NBC affiliate. Another 2026 case involved Delta State University student Demartravion Reed in Mississippi. Officials "determined the cause of death to be a hanging and the manner of death as suicide." At the time, the case reopened old memories of the murder of Emmett Till, according to reports. Till was a Black teen kidnapped and murdered by White men not far from the site after he was falsely accused of flirting with a White woman in 1955. 15-YEAR-OLD BLACK TEEN'S MURDER REVEALS THE UGLY TRUTH ABOUT WHITE GUILT IN AMERICA A Grio report on Pressley’s letter also referenced the hanging deaths of a 58-year-old man in Albany, N.Y., and a 39-year-old man in Brookfield, Wisconsin. The Albany Police Department said Earl Smith’s death was "ruled a suicide" and investigators found "no evidence" of criminal activity. "The Albany Police Department is aware of concerns posted on social media suggesting that criminal activity was involved with this incident, which has understandably caused public concern," the department said. A preliminary investigation of the Wisconsin man’s death also indicated suicide, according to Brookfield’s police chief cited by the Waukesha County Freeman. At least one case remains under homicide investigation, according to reports. Tasia Fortune was found hanging outside an abandoned house in Jackson, Mississippi, CNN reported Thursday. Authorities later questioned Terence Bernard Anderson, the father of one of her children, and arrested him on unrelated weapons charges, according to several reports. AOC SLAMS ‘OPPRESSED’ TRUMP STATES WHILE TOUTING NYC SERVICES DESPITE $5B DEFICIT AND TRANSIT CRIME SPIKE The lawmakers’ characterization also drew criticism on social media. "Those community notes are stacking up," one critic said, as X’s crowdsourced correction indicator included several wire reports and media links disputing Ocasio-Cortez’ claims. "There should be some sort of penalty for willfully lying on social media, especially for a politician," another claimed. Former Energy Department official Matt Van Swol posted to X, "In the last ‘lynching’ of a Black woman, the media conveniently left out the prime suspect in the case was her Black boyfriend. Zero White people are lynching Black people in America today." WATCH: SQUAD DEMOCRAT SPEAKS OUT AFTER TEEN FOUND SHOT DEAD AT HUSBAND’S BOSTON PROPERTY Former Senate staffer Matt Whitlock added that "every death is a tragedy, but what do you think ‘widespread’ means if only one of these was actually a homicide. Not sure you’ve landed the point about ‘racial terror’ with this." X’s crowdsourced Community Notes feature also pointed readers to law-enforcement and medical-examiner findings in several of the cases, stating that most high-profile hanging deaths it identified in 2025 and 2026 had been ruled suicides and that one remained under homicide investigation. articles.title: 9/11 widow Terry Strada accuses US of protecting Saudi Arabia 25 years after terror attacks, addresses Vance
articles.summary: Terry Strada accused the U.S. government of protecting Saudi Arabia and urged JD Vance to carry her message of accountability back to Trump.
articles.body: Terry Strada, whose husband was killed in the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, said Friday during the 25th anniversary ceremony at Ground Zero that Saudi Arabia continues to evade responsibility for the terrorist attacks. Strada went on to accuse the U.S. government of "protecting" Saudi Arabia, saying "administration after administration" had failed the victims' families over the last quarter-century. "The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia fomented a rancid culture of anti-American terrorism around the globe, and then sent its agents to support the radical Islamist hijackers so they could attack you and all of our loved ones," said Strada, the national chair of 9/11 Families United. "But for 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," Strada added. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES She also addressed Vice President JD Vance, the most senior Trump administration official to attend the ceremony in Lower Manhattan. President Donald Trump spoke at the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. "It has been one betrayal after another. President Trump can still change that. Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this," Strada said. "Vice President Vance, thank you for being here today. Please carry that message back. Stand with the families. Stand with the survivors. Stand with Americans." Strada's husband, Tom Strada, was on the 104th floor of the North Tower when it was struck by American Airlines Flight 11, Strada told WPTV in an interview on the 20th anniversary of 9/11. Tom Strada, 41, worked at Cantor Fitzgerald and days before attacks, he and his wife had brought their third child home from the hospital. After the impact of the plane, he called her and said he was heading toward the stairwell. 9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY Since her husband's death, along with the deaths of nearly 3,000 others at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and aboard the hijacked planes, Strada has become a leading advocate for accountability and transparency surrounding the Sept. 11 attacks. Strada is among thousands of Sept. 11 family members and survivors who sued Saudi Arabia, alleging the kingdom provided material support to the al Qaeda hijackers. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly denied the allegations. During her remarks Friday, Strada reminded the crowd that a federal judge ruled last August there was "reasonable evidence" that two Saudi government employees supported two future al-Qaeda hijackers who came to the United States in early 2000 and took flight lessons. The judge, George B. Daniels, allowed the lawsuit to go forward, denying Saudi Arabia's attempt to dismiss it. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For more than a decade after the Sept. 11 attacks, victims' families were barred from pursuing a lawsuit against a foreign government because of sovereign immunity protections. That changed in September 2016, when Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), allowing Americans to sue foreign governments accused of providing material support for terrorist attacks on U.S. soil. In her speech, Strada criticized President Barack Obama for vetoing JASTA. At the time, he argued the legislation went too far by threatening "to strip all foreign governments of immunity from judicial process in the United States based solely upon allegations by private litigants." Congress overrode his veto days later, making JASTA law and paving the way for the lawsuit against Saudi Arabia to be filed in March 2017. The case remains pending in federal court.
